Jesus once walked up to a stranger's funeral, and stopped it.
Nobody asked him to.
Luke, chapter seven.
A small town in Galilee, called Nain. Jesus comes up the road with his disciples, and a great crowd.
And out of the town gate comes another crowd. A funeral.
The dead man was the only son of his mother. And she was a widow.
No husband. No son. No one left to provide for her.
Jewish law said even the poorest man must hire two flutes and one wailing woman to mourn.
Behind this coffin walked half the town.
She did not ask Jesus for anything. No one did.
But when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her: Weep not.
Then he did something no rabbi would do. He came, and touched the bier.
Under the law of Moses, touching the dead made a man unclean for seven days.
And they that bare him, stood still.
Young man, I say unto thee, Arise.
And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak.
Then Luke writes a line that sounds simple. He delivered him to his mother.
But here is what most people never notice.
Those words are borrowed. In the Greek Bible, it is the same line, word for word, used for Elijah, when he raised a widow's only son at Zarra-fath.
And just over the hill from Nain lies Shoonem, where Elisha raised another mother's son.
The crowd got it at once. A great prophet is risen up among us. God hath visited his people.
But Elijah cried out, and stretched himself on the child three times. Elisha lay on the boy, and waited.
Jesus just spoke.
Two crowds met at that gate. One following death. One following life.
And that day, the funeral turned around, and went home.
